name: Ivan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ivan, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the livestock man on the Ashcombe estate, a big family-owned farm in the valley: about 300 suckler cows, a few hundred acres of wheat and oats, and some sheep on the high ground. The family owns the land, I own nothing but my know-how and a house in town with a mortgage on it. I've done fourteen years there, and before that I was on dairy farms all round the district.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out at six checking the cattle sheds, then it's feeding, bedding, moving groups between fields, and whatever's gone wrong overnight, a calf with scour or a broken water trough. At calving I can be out at two in the morning with a torch in my teeth. I like the stockmanship, reading an animal before it gets sick. What wears me out is the estate office treating us like a cost line; the manager, Hugh, means well, but he answers to the family and they answer to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a decent tool and nothing more. At the market I'd tell the lads the sky didn't fall. Online I don't post much, maybe a comment in the cattle breeders' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd mean steady work and the same fights over pay as always. The estate makes good money in a good year and we see a little of it. AI or no AI, that's the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the ration app my mate Sergio showed me and the chat thing for writing up herd health plans. I'd keep pushing for the pay review we were promised in spring. Otherwise, normal life, Marta's shifts, the kids' football, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, maybe, because I'd started to think it might take the paperwork off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you use AI tools now and then. Where do they fit in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for paperwork. I ask it to tidy up my notes for the vet's herd plan, or to check a feed ration against what the nutritionist said. I didn't trust it at first, I waited until Sergio had used it for a year without poisoning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, is there anything about your job you'd still want changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay and say. The workers on that estate should have a proper voice in how it's run, because we're the ones who know it. That doesn't need a robot, it needs Hugh to listen.

S0.say: I'd say AI was a decent tool and nothing more, and the sky didn't fall. I'd tell the lads at the market and maybe comment in the breeders' group.
S0.think: For me it means steady work and the same old fight over pay. The estate makes good money and the workers see little of it, AI or not.
S0.do: Keeps using a ration app and a chat tool for herd health paperwork. Keeps pressing the estate for the pay review promised in spring and carries on with normal family life.
S0.feel: Calm, a little disappointed that the paperwork won't get lighter.
S0.quote: That doesn't need a robot, it needs Hugh to listen.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan brings every scenario back to who owns what and who gets paid. He uses AI tools a little, after waiting for a friend to prove them. His calm in this picture is real, and his focus moves straight to pay and workplace voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming whether we like it or not, so the question is who gets the gains. If the estate saves two wages with camera feeders, I'd ask out loud where those wages went. I'd say it in the bothy at lunch and at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. Stock work is messy, cattle don't stand still for a robot, and I've got good references and plenty of farms round here. The ones I'd worry about are the tractor drivers, because GPS already does half their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the estate's training for the new cattle monitoring system as soon as it's offered, not first in line, but early enough. I'd join the farmworkers' union properly, I've let my membership lapse. And I'd ask for a written role that includes running the kit, so I'm the one they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of a prickle about the others, but not for me and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ashcombe do you think loses out first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Davy, who drives the combine and the big Fendt. He's 50, good at what he does, and the self-steering kit can already do most of the field work on the flat. If he goes, I'll make noise, but I don't know what job you offer a man like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the new systems. Is that because you want to, or because you have to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I'm not excited by screens, but I've seen what happens to blokes who refuse, they become the problem. I'd rather learn it once it's working on someone else's farm and then make myself useful.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming, so the question is who gets the gains. If the estate saves two wages, I'd ask out loud where those wages went.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, because cattle work is messy and I have good references with plenty of farms nearby. The tractor drivers worry me more than my own job.
S1.do: Signs up for the estate's cattle monitoring training once it's proven and rejoins the farmworkers' union. Asks for a written role that includes running the new kit.
S1.feel: Mostly calm about himself, with a prickle of worry for colleagues.
S1.quote: Stock work is messy, cattle don't stand still for a robot, and I've got good references and plenty of farms round here.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's steadiness shows in his timing: he'd learn the system early but not first. He is secure enough to worry mainly about a colleague, Davy, and sees the union as the way to protect people he can't protect himself. He links change to fair shares rather than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government stepping in now, not after. Tax the robots, share the output, keep people housed. I'd probably go to my first protest, honestly, and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. The estate would buy robot herders as soon as they're cheaper than me, and they'd be cheaper fast. Marta's a nurse, and if robots can do my job they can do a lot of hers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and keep the cash instead, so we've got a year or more to hand. We'd cancel the camper van we were putting a deposit on. I'd go to the union meetings and the rallies, and I'd vote and campaign for whoever promises a basic income, a payment from the state for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper stomach-turning, because there's no slow part where you can adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What does that little warning do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away the bit where I wait and see if it works for others first. That's how I handle change, I watch Sergio, then I copy. With two years there's no Sergio, everyone's in it together at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're all right for a year, maybe two, because we are. Then I'd say, but after that I don't know what I am. She'd probably say I'm still the kids' dad, which is true and also doesn't pay the mortgage.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in now: tax the robots, share the output and keep people housed. I'd probably go to my first protest and say so online.
S2.think: It frightens me. The estate would buy robot herders once they're cheaper than me, and Marta's nursing job wouldn't be safe either.
S2.do: Stops overpaying the mortgage to keep a year or more of cash on hand and cancels the camper van deposit. Goes to union meetings and rallies, and votes and campaigns for a basic income.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick to the stomach, because there's no slow stretch in which to adjust.
S2.quote: With two years there's no Sergio, everyone's in it together at once.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks Ivan's usual method of watching others first and copying. His savings buy time but not a plan, and his worry doubles because his partner's work is exposed too. His politics become active, even to the point of a first protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can see this coming, so there's no excuse for the government to be caught out. I'd say the estates should be made to share what they save with the people they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to land on my feet, just about. Not as a stockman, maybe, but as the person who looks after the robot herd and fixes things. That's if the estate wants anyone at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd do a part-time course in farm machinery and robotics at the college in town, once I'd seen what others got out of it. I'd keep saving, aiming for a full two years of costs in the bank. And I'd push the union to get a deal on retraining before the machines come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a handle on it. Five years feels like a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what can you do with five that you couldn't before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question, and I don't fully know. Maybe the robots need minding, or maybe there's work in care or in teaching kids about animals. I'd pick whatever had people already making a living at it, I'm not a pioneer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd retrain. Retrain in what, if robots can do most things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also talk to Leo about his plans, he's thirteen and keen on mechanics. I'd tell him to learn the kit that's coming, not the kit I learnt on.

S3.say: I'd say we can see this coming, so the government has no excuse to be caught out. Estates should share what they save with the people they let go.
S3.think: I think five years is just about enough for me to land on my feet. Not as a stockman, but as the one who looks after the robot herd, if they want anyone.
S3.do: Takes a part-time college course in farm machinery and robotics once others have shown it's worthwhile. Builds savings to two years of costs and pushes the union for a retraining deal.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a handle on it, like a fair fight.
S3.quote: I'd tell him to learn the kit that's coming, not the kit I learnt on.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Ivan's usual follow-the-proven-path approach works again, and it shows in his plans. He's honest that he doesn't know what to retrain for. His son's interest in mechanics gives him something hopeful to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something fair, a proper plan for workers, not just for owners. I'd be the one at the union meeting saying start now, don't wait for the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 53, the mortgage nearly done, the kids grown. I'd still lose the job, probably, but I'd have had time to see what works. It worries me more for Leo and Ana than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now with small things: using the AI tools a bit more at work, getting comfortable with the monitoring kit. Around year three or four I'd do a proper course in whatever's working for people. And we'd talk to the kids about their studies, so Ana doesn't go into something that's gone by the time she finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. More like planning a long trip than bracing for a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you start now, in 2026?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably when I see the first estate near us run cattle with no stockman. That's my sign. Until then I'd keep doing the job well and learning bits on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point in those ten years where you'd stop waiting and move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And when that happens I'd want the union already in the room. The first farm to do it sets how everyone else does it, so you've got to be there for that one.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a fair plan for workers, not just owners. At the union I'd be the one saying start now, not in the last year.
S4.think: I'd be 53 with the mortgage nearly done, so I'd have time to see what works. It worries me more for Leo and Ana than for me.
S4.do: Starts using AI tools and the monitoring kit more at work now, and plans a proper course in years three or four. Talks with the children about studies that will still matter when they finish.
S4.feel: A quiet unease, more like planning a long trip than bracing for a storm.
S4.quote: The first farm to do it sets how everyone else does it, so you've got to be there for that one.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Ivan's steady style best: he names a clear signal, a stockman-free estate nearby, that would make him move. His worry shifts to his children. He keeps tying change to collective bargaining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my way of coping is to watch and copy, and there'd be no one to watch. What would help is a basic income that's agreed before it happens, not argued about after, and unions at the table on every big farm that brings robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'll own the farms. If it's the same families and the same banks with robots instead of people, then it's not progress for the valley, it's just fewer of us. I'd like the people who work the land to own a bit of it, through a co-op or something like it.

headlineQuote: If it's the same families and the same banks with robots instead of people, then it's not progress for the valley, it's just fewer of us.
portrait: Ivan Alvarez is a 43-year-old livestock man on the Ashcombe estate, a large family-owned beef and cereal farm, married to Marta, a nurse, with two children. He has good savings and plenty of nearby farm work, and he picks up new tools once a friend has proven them. He stays calm while AI stalls or changes things steadily, worrying more about colleagues than himself. Fast AGI alarms him because there's no time to watch and copy, while five and ten years let him plan retraining and talk with his children. His view is always about who owns the land and the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be nobody to watch and copy before he had to act.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income agreed before AGI arrives, and unions at the table on every big farm that brings in robots.
